title: Bagel with Lox
subtitle: A plain or seeded bagel spread with cream cheese, cold-smoked salmon, and all the trimmings
excerpt: The New York deli classic: a toasted bagel spread generously with cream cheese, layered with cold-smoked salmon, sliced red onion, capers, dill, and a squeeze of lemon. No cooking required, and it takes ten minutes from fridge to plate.
sourceNotes: The bagel with cream cheese and smoked salmon is a staple of New York Jewish deli culture, popularised by Eastern European Jewish immigrants in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The term 'lox' specifically refers to brine-cured salmon; in common deli usage it now encompasses cold-smoked salmon as well.

content.text: A bagel with lox is a lesson in restraint and proportion. The bagel carries the cream cheese; the cream cheese carries the salmon; the onion and capers and dill cut through the richness with acidity, sharpness, and freshness. Get those proportions right and the result is one of the finest things you can eat at eleven in the morning. The only cooking involved is toasting the bagel, which is optional, some people prefer them untoasted, particularly if the bagel is very fresh, and the whole thing comes together in under ten minutes.

Strictly speaking, {{smoked-salmon}} lox is brine-cured salmon that has not been smoked. The name comes from the Yiddish word for salmon, 'laks'. What most delis and supermarkets now sell as lox is cold-smoked salmon: cured in salt and sugar, then briefly cold-smoked at a low temperature (below 30°C) so it stays raw in texture. This is the silky, deep-orange, thinly-sliced product found at every supermarket fish counter. That's what you want here. Hot-smoked salmon (the flaky kind) is a different product and doesn't work well in this assembly. It's too dry and breaks apart rather than draping.

Halve the {{bagel}} bagels and toast if desired, a toasted bagel gives textural contrast to the soft cream cheese and salmon; an untoasted one is chewier and more substantial. Spread each half generously with {{cream-cheese}} cream cheese. The layer should be thick enough to see under the salmon: roughly 25 g per half, pressed into the bread rather than just balanced on top.

Lay the {{smoked-salmon}} smoked salmon over the cream cheese in overlapping folds, don't lay it flat. Folding it gives more texture and means you get varying thickness in each bite. Scatter the finely sliced {{red-onion}} red onion over the salmon. The slices should be thin enough to be almost translucent; a mandoline or a sharp knife and patience both work. Add the drained {{capers}} capers and scatter over the fresh {{dill}} dill.

Squeeze the {{lemon}} lemon generously over the top and add several turns of freshly cracked {{black-pepper}} black pepper. No salt: the salmon, capers, and cream cheese are already sufficiently seasoned.

A bagel with too little cream cheese is a dry sandwich. Use more than you think is reasonable. A bagel with too little salmon is disappointing. The quantities here give you 30 g salmon per bagel half, roughly three thin slices, which is the minimum. The lemon is not optional; without acid, the dish is cloying.

The bagel with cream cheese and smoked salmon is one of the defining foods of New York Jewish deli culture. Eastern European Jewish immigrants brought bagel-baking traditions to the Lower East Side of Manhattan in the late 19th century. By the early 20th century, the pairing with cream cheese and lox was established. The bagel delis of Second Avenue and Delancey Street were serving them to queues out the door. The tradition spread across America through the mid-20th century and eventually to the UK, where supermarket bagels and pre-sliced smoked salmon made it a standard weekend brunch. The best versions are still found in dedicated bagel shops: hand-rolled, boiled before baking, and dense and chewy in a way that factory bagels rarely match.
